cards.back: Guillermo del Toro, 2006, Spain/Mexico co-production.

cards.front: When and where is Pan’s Labyrinth set?
cards.back: 1944, northern Spain, five years after the Civil War, as Franco’s forces hunt guerrillas.
Guillermo Navarro, who won the Oscar for Best Cinematography.
Cinematography, Art Direction and Makeup.

cards.front: Budget and gross of Pan’s Labyrinth?
cards.back: About $19 million budget; about $83 million worldwide.
Javier Navarrete.

cards.front: Who plays the Faun and the Pale Man?
cards.back: Doug Jones, in prosthetics.

cards.front: What does the pile of shoes in the Pale Man’s lair evoke?
cards.back: The Holocaust: victims of a devouring elite.

cards.front: What does Mercedes tell Vidal before he dies?
cards.back: His son will not even know his name.
A flower on a dead branch: imagination and innocence survive.
“She is just a woman.”
The Devil’s Backbone (2001), also set in the Spanish Civil War.
Cold blue-grey for the fascist reality; warm amber-gold for the fantasy.

cards.front: Three techniques in the bottle murder?
cards.back: Low-key lighting, no musical build-up, exaggerated (sweetened) sound.

cards.front: City of God: directors, year, country?
cards.back: Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund, 2002, Brazil.

cards.front: What is City of God based on?
cards.back: Paulo Lins’ novel about the real Cidade de Deus housing project.
César Charlone.
Daniel Rezende.

cards.front: How many Oscar nominations did City of God receive?
cards.back: Four, including Best Director and Best Cinematography.

cards.front: Bentes’ critique of City of God?
cards.back: A “cosmetics of hunger”: poverty made slick and glossy.
“An Aesthetic of Hunger” (1965).

cards.front: Rocket’s line about the favela trap?
cards.back: “If you run, the beast gets you; if you stay, the beast eats you.”

cards.front: Three techniques in the chicken chase?
cards.back: Handheld camera, rapid editing, a 360° spin back in time.

cards.front: What does the Story of the Apartment show?
cards.back: The cycle: the flat stays, the dealers keep dying and being replaced.

cards.front: Which photo does Rocket choose to publish?
cards.back: The dead Li’l Zé, not the corrupt police: his career over the truth.

cards.front: How does City of God’s colour change over time?
cards.back: Warm golden 1960s; colder, darker 1980s.
Asif Kapadia, produced by James Gay-Rees, 2015.
Oscar and BAFTA for Best Documentary; also a Grammy for Best Music Film.
Senna (2010), about the F1 driver Ayrton Senna.
Audio only, laid over archive footage: no talking heads.

cards.front: Who edited Amy and who composed its score?
cards.back: Chris King (editor), Antonio Pinto (score).

cards.front: Who objected to Amy and why?
cards.back: Mitch Winehouse: he said it was misleading about him.

cards.front: What distinctive text appears on screen?
cards.back: Amy’s handwritten lyrics as she sings.
Belgrade, weeks before her death.

cards.front: When and how did Amy Winehouse die?
cards.back: July 2011, aged 27, from alcohol poisoning.

cards.front: Why is Amy a digital-era documentary?
cards.back: Its footage comes from camcorders, phones and digital press cameras.
Compilation documentary and rise-and-fall structure existed long before digital.
The “monoform”: mainstream media’s fast, fragmented, single-voice style.
Culloden (1964) and The War Game (1965).
Kurt and Courtney (1998); Whitney: Can I Be Me (2017).
Invisible filmmaker, no voiceover or captions, fiction-like identification, no conclusions.
Bowling for Columbine (2002) and Fahrenheit 9/11 (2004).
“The creative treatment of actuality.”
Poetic, expository, observational, participatory, reflexive, performative.
Diegetic exists in the story world; non-diegetic is heard only by the audience.
Deep keeps all planes sharp; shallow isolates one plane.
